The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: record.save inside validation re-runs BlockedEmail validations (including a uniqueness query) on the hot signup path

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, blocked emails trigger `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. That method loads a matching `BlockedEmail` and then updates stats via `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Since `BlockedEmail` has `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`, `save` will run validations (including the uniqueness lookup) on each blocked-signup attempt, adding avoidable DB work on the signup validation path. This is a performance/architecture concern rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? invoked from User#valid? can cause persistence failures inside code paths that must not persist, raising ActiveRecord errors and surfacing as a 500 instead of a validation error

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator#validate_each` which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `should_block?` performs a DB write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save`) as part of validation. This introduces side effects during `User` validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), meaning merely calling `user.valid?` can mutate `blocked_emails` and can do so even if the user later fails other validations. While the finding’s claim about 500s from ActiveRecord exceptions isn’t directly proven by the diff (since `save` is non-bang and there’s no demonstrated exception path), the underlying concern—persisting inside validation paths that are expected to be side-effect free—is real and directly grounded in the changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail matching is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and unique index compare raw strings), so blocking can be bypassed by registering with different case variation

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` looks up `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and the table has a unique index on the raw `email` string. There’s no normalization (e.g., `downcase`) on insert or lookup, so a blocked entry for `block@spam.com` would not match `Block@Spam.com` on case-sensitive databases/indices, allowing a case-variation bypass of the block check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test covers case variation in blocked-email matching

adjudication.rationale: The added blocked-email logic matches by exact string equality (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value`). The new specs (`spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`, `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) only test exact-case matches and do not cover case-variant inputs (e.g., stored `block@x.com` vs submitted `BLOCK@x.com`). This is a specific, diff-grounded missing edge-case test rather than a proven defect in the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No writer for blocked_emails exists in the diff (no admin UI, API, rake task, seed, or documented path), making the feature unusable as shipped

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `blocked_emails` table (migration), a `BlockedEmail` model, and wires it into signup via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but it does not add any controller, admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or other in-app mechanism to create/manage `BlockedEmail` records. That makes the feature operational only if records are inserted out-of-band (e.g., DB/console), which is a legitimate completeness/maintainability concern, though not a direct runtime defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No tests verify the new controller JSON response contract (errors:/values: keys) in users_controller.rb

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `UsersController#create` failure JSON to include new `errors` and `values` keys (users_controller.rb render json ... `errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: user.attributes.slice(...)`), and the Ember controller now relies on those keys (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) ...`). The added specs cover `BlockedEmail` and `EmailValidator`, but there are no controller/request specs in the diff asserting the new JSON response shape, so this new response contract is untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No tests cover the rejected-emails client validation state machine and the result.errors.email && result.values guard in create_account_controller.js

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side state/logic in create_account_controller.js (rejectedEmails array, contains(email) check in emailValidation, dependency on 'rejectedEmails.@each', and the failure-path guard `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... }`). The only tests added in the diff are Ruby specs for EmailValidator and BlockedEmail; there are no JS/client tests shown that exercise this new rejectedEmails validation flow or the specific guard behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator never checks syntactic validity of the email, allowing garbage addresses like 'user@' or 'not-an-email' to pass when domain settings are blank

adjudication.rationale: In `User` the only non-presence/uniqueness email validation is now `validates :email, email: true` (i.e., `EmailValidator`). The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` only enforces whitelist/blacklist domain restrictions and `BlockedEmail.should_block?`; it contains no syntactic/format check for the email string when those settings are blank, so values like `user@` or `not-an-email` would not be rejected by this validator.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client displays the wrong error for a blocked email: field validation hardcodes 'user.email.invalid' instead of the new 'user.email.blocked' locale key, showing contradictory messages

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new `rejectedEmails` mechanism marks an email as invalid on subsequent validations, but it hardcodes the reason to `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (see the `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` branch). The server-side change introduces a distinct blocked-email validation message (`I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` in `EmailValidator` and `user.email.blocked` locale key), and the controller now pushes any server-returned email error into `rejectedEmails` (`result.errors.email`). This means a *blocked* email (or other server-side email error) will be shown client-side as “invalid”, contradicting the new specific blocked message.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-email validation gated on email_changed? means emails blocked after account creation are never re-checked on ordinary saves, and should_block? stats only tick on create

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb`, the new validator is wired as `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so `EmailValidator` (which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`) only runs when the email changes (including on create). That means if an email gets added to `blocked_emails` after a user is created, ordinary saves that don’t modify `email` won’t re-check it, and the `match_count/last_match_at` stats in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` will only update on creates or email-change events. Whether that’s desired is a product/behavior question, but the finding is accurately grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_emails table has no writer in the codebase — no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed inserts BlockedEmail rows, so the block-emails feature is unreachable end-to-end

adjudication.rationale: From this diff alone you can see BlockedEmail is only read via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in the new `EmailValidator`, and there’s no new code here that creates/updates `BlockedEmail` rows outside of tests/fabricators. However, the finding claims *the entire codebase* has no writer/admin UI/API/rake/seed, which cannot be verified from a PR diff snippet (those could exist unchanged elsewhere).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client discards the server's distinct blocked-email error and shows generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') instead of user.email.blocked on the modal path

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, when an email has been rejected once (`rejectedEmails.contains(email)`), the client-side validation always returns `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (new block at lines ~65-73), regardless of the server-provided error. Meanwhile the server can now produce a distinct blocked-email message via `EmailValidator` (`record.errors.add(attribute, I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked'))`). The failure handler pushes the rejected email whenever `result.errors.email` exists (lines ~271-275) but does not preserve or display the specific `user.email.blocked` reason; subsequent validations show the generic `user.email.invalid` instead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Controller returns errors/values payload where only the email error is consumed; errors hash broadcast to all failed signups with no consumer (payload/API scope drift)

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON payload is expanded to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. On the client side, `create_account_controller.js` only consumes this new structure to check `result.errors.email` and then push `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails`; nothing in this diff uses other keys in `errors` or `values`. That’s a concrete API/payload expansion beyond the demonstrated consumer need (scope drift / broader API surface), but not a verifiable correctness bug by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs read-then-write (match_count += 1; record.save) inside a model validation hook — side effect in a pure-seeming validation, persists even when caller validates without saving

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `BlockedEmail.should_block?` doing a DB write (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) and this method is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs as part of `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `User` (i.e., during model validation). That means simply running validations (e.g., `user.valid?`, or a failed save due to other errors) can still persist side effects to `blocked_emails`, which is an architectural/behavioral concern (unexpected writes during validation, stats can increment even when the user record never saves), though not necessarily a functional defect if intended for tracking.

adjudication_records.issue_text: match_count write fires even when action_type == :do_nothing, writing DB for a decision not to act; stats tracking not in stated intent and match_count/last_match_at never consumed

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` and `save`s whenever a record exists, regardless of `action_type` (see `if record ... record.save` before returning `record.action_type == actions[:block]`). This means even `:do_nothing` causes a DB write; additionally the method is a predicate with side effects. The claim that these stats are "never consumed" isn’t verifiable from the diff, but the unconditional writes/perf/semantics concern is real and diff-grounded (and is even asserted in specs for both action types).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Refactor stacks EachValidator after uniqueness with errors[attribute].blank? guard so blocked-email check is skipped when presence/uniqueness already failed, with no spec coverage for these paths

adjudication.rationale: In `User` the email validations are declared as `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` followed by `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so `EmailValidator#validate_each` will typically run after presence/uniqueness. Inside the validator it explicitly guards the blocked-email check with `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, meaning blocked-email matching/stat updates are skipped whenever a prior validator already added an email error (e.g., blank/duplicate). The added specs (`email_validator_spec.rb`) only cover the blocked vs not-blocked paths with a clean record and do not cover cases where `record.errors[:email]` is already populated, so those guarded paths are untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No integration spec proving a User with a blocked email fails user.save; only test stubs should_block? so user.rb wiring is never exercised

adjudication.rationale: The diff wires blocked-email logic into User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (app/models/user.rb) and implements `EmailValidator` to call `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). However, the only validator spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` directly (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) and there is no spec that exercises the end-to-end wiring by attempting `user.save`/`user.valid?` with a blocked email and asserting the User model fails validation due to the validator being invoked. This is a concrete missing-test gap for new behavior, not a verified runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitive exact-match lookup in BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and the unique index on blocked_emails.email bypasses the email block for mixed-case variants (no canonicalization/downcasing on read or write paths), and the unique index permits both casings as separate rows

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and the model/index store `email` as-is (no downcasing/canonicalization in `set_defaults` or elsewhere). The migration adds a plain unique index on `blocked_emails.email` and the model validates `uniqueness: true` without `case_sensitive: false`, so mixed-case variants can be stored as distinct rows and won’t match each other on lookup in case-sensitive DBs, allowing blocked emails to bypass via casing changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs record.save inside EmailValidator#validate_each, so match_count and last_match_at are incremented on every valid? call, corrupting the stats whenever validation runs multiple times or is called for unrelated purposes

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) whenever there are no prior errors for that attribute. BlockedEmail.should_block? (app/models/blocked_email.rb) has side effects: it increments match_count, sets last_match_at, and calls record.save whenever a matching record exists. Since model validations can run multiple times per request/lifecycle (e.g., repeated valid? calls, validations triggered by form re-render, or other unrelated validations), this will inflate/corrupt the blocked email statistics independent of a definitive “block” event.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Counter update uses read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) instead of an atomic UPDATE increment, causing lost updates under concurrent signups from the same blocked address

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does `record.match_count += 1` and then `record.save` after fetching the row (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`). This is a classic read-modify-write sequence that is not atomic; concurrent signups hitting the same `blocked_emails.email` can overwrite each other’s increments, causing lost updates to `match_count` (and potentially `last_match_at` ordering). An atomic SQL increment (e.g., `update_counters`/`UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`) would avoid this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The BlockedEmail table ships with no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path), so the feature is dead code and operators cannot block an email without opening a Rails console

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `BlockedEmail` is introduced (model + migration) and enforced via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but there is no corresponding creation/management path added here (no controller/admin UI/seed/rake task in the shown changes) aside from test fabricators. That makes the feature operationally incomplete in the scope of this PR, even if it can still work when the table is populated out-of-band (e.g., console/manual SQL).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails cache in create_account_controller.js grows unbounded and is never cleared, so a transient email error permanently rejects subsequent attempts with the generic 'invalid' message and never consults the server again, leaving the correct 'blocked' server-side message unsurfaced

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a persistent `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` cache and short-circuits `emailValidation` to immediately fail with `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` (create_account_controller.js). Entries are added on any failed create that includes `result.errors.email` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), and nothing in the diff clears or bounds this array. This can cause subsequent attempts with the same email to be rejected client-side with a generic “invalid” reason regardless of the original server-side error (e.g., `user.email.blocked` added in server.en.yml), and the cache can grow without limit during the controller’s lifetime. Whether it fully prevents re-submission/server re-check depends on surrounding submit/disable logic not shown here, so the “never consults the server again” part isn’t fully verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client caches rejected emails permanently in rejectedEmails, so emails that fail validation once can never be resubmitted without a page reload even if the server would now accept them

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, failed account creation pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` when `result.errors.email` is present. The `emailValidation` computed property then hard-fails any email contained in `rejectedEmails` (`contains(email)`), returning a validation failure without rechecking the server. Nothing in the diff ever removes/clears `rejectedEmails`, so within the lifetime of this controller (until reload/modal teardown) the same email can never be resubmitted even if server-side conditions change and it would now pass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client displays I18n.t('user.email.invalid') which misrepresents the actual server rejection reason (e.g., server says 'not allowed' but user sees 'invalid')

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, if the email is in `rejectedEmails`, `emailMatch` returns a failed `InputValidation` with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (lines adding the `contains` check). The controller populates `rejectedEmails` for any server response that has `result.errors.email` (regardless of whether the server error is `user.email.not_allowed`, `user.email.blocked`, uniqueness, etc.). Since the server now returns structured `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and also adds a new `user.email.blocked` message, the client still collapses all such rejections into the generic 'invalid' inline message, which can misrepresent the actual server rejection reason.

adjudication_records.issue_text: rejectedEmails blocklist is never cleared anywhere in the diff

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails` is introduced (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`) and populated on failed signup (`pushObject(result.values.email)` when `result.errors.email` is present). The email validation then hard-fails if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`. There is no code in this diff that ever clears or resets `rejectedEmails` (other than implicit controller teardown outside the diff), so within the lifetime of the controller the client will permanently block any previously-rejected email value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: users_controller.rb error payload echoes back raw user input (name, username, email) on every failed account creation, leaking PII beyond the feature's intent

adjudication.rationale: In `users_controller.rb#create`, the failure JSON response was changed to always include `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` along with `errors: user.errors.to_hash`. This echoes back user-supplied PII (including email) on any failed account creation, which is an expansion of the error payload and can be considered an information disclosure/privacy issue relative to the prior behavior (only `message`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: users_controller.rb leaks errors.to_hash with internal error keys for all validations, not just email blocking, changing the response contract for every failure path

adjudication.rationale: In `users_controller.rb#create`, the failure JSON response was expanded from only `message` to also include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. This is a response-contract change for all create failures (not limited to email blocking) and exposes the full validation error hash keyed by attribute names. The client change only checks `result.errors.email`, but the controller now returns all errors unconditionally, which may be broader than necessary and could affect other consumers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Refactored validation grouping in user.rb combines presence, uniqueness, and email validators on one line, so future edits adding an option will silently apply it to all three checks

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not combine presence, uniqueness, and the email-format validator into a single `validates` call. It uses `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` and separately `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. The finding’s claim about an option silently applying to all three checks is not grounded in the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? is gated behind if: :email_changed?, so blocked emails are only checked at signup/email-change and never re-validated for existing users with blocked stored emails

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb`, the new blocked-email check lives inside the `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), and that validator is only run via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. That means existing users whose `email` is already persisted will not be re-validated against newly-added `BlockedEmail` entries on later saves unless they change their email. This matches the finding, but it’s more a scope/behavior decision than a verifiable defect from the diff alone (the previous domain blacklist/whitelist validator was also gated by `email_changed?`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: No spec covers the email_changed? gating of the blocked-email path, leaving the accepted intent undocumented

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces conditional validation in `User`: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (replacing the prior `validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`). The new `EmailValidator` contains the blocked-email logic (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but the added specs either unit-test `EmailValidator#validate_each` directly (bypassing the `email_changed?` condition) or test `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in isolation. No spec in the diff exercises a `User` instance where `email_changed?` is false/true to document whether blocked-email checks run only on email changes. This is a concrete test gap about the intended gating, not a proven runtime defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unanchored substring regex in email_validator.rb lets domain whitelist/blacklist be bypassed via domain embedding (e.g. user@example.com.attacker.tld passes whitelist)
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core flaw: the domain-matching regex is not properly anchored/boundary-checked, so a whitelisted domain like example.com can be bypassed by using a larger domain that contains it (e.g., evil.example.com or example.com.attacker.tld).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blacklist bypass via subdomains since regex requires @ immediately before the domain (user@foo.spam.com doesn't match @spam\.com)

adjudication.rationale: `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` (same logic as the removed `User#email_in_restriction_setting?`). This only matches when the restricted domain appears immediately after `@`, so a blacklist entry like `spam.com` will not match `user@foo.spam.com`, allowing subdomain bypass of the domain restriction.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is an exact case-sensitive match, so blocking is bypassed by varying email casing (no normalization like downcasing)

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization (e.g., downcasing) and the `blocked_emails.email` column is a plain string. In common deployments (e.g., PostgreSQL), this equality match is case-sensitive, so a blocked entry like `bad@spam.com` would not match `Bad@Spam.com`, allowing bypass by changing casing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs unconditional read-modify-write on the unauthenticated signup path, allowing unauthenticated attackers to poison match_count/last_match_at statistics and cause lock contention

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, a matching record is always updated (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = Time.zone.now`, `save`) on every validation attempt (read-modify-write), regardless of authentication. This method is invoked from the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) which is wired into `User` validations (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`) and therefore runs on the unauthenticated signup path (`UsersController#create`). An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly submit a blocked email to inflate `match_count`/`last_match_at` (“poison” stats) and generate DB write load/row lock contention on that `blocked_emails` row.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Regex interpolation of SiteSetting email domain whitelist/blacklist values with only '.' escaped allows metacharacters to change matching semantics and enables ReDoS via catastrophic backtracking on the unauthenticated signup endpoint

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?`, the regex is built via `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` is derived from a SiteSetting with only `.` escaped (`setting.gsub('.', '\\.')`). Any other regex metacharacters in the whitelist/blacklist (e.g., `|`, `()`, `+`, `*`, `{}`) will be interpreted as regex, changing matching semantics (possible bypass/overmatch) and can create pathological regexes that may be expensive to evaluate against attacker-controlled signup emails on an unauthenticated endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New email_validator_spec only covers the BlockedEmail.should_block? branch and none of the whitelist/blacklist logic relocated from user.rb into lib/validators/email_validator.rb, since both tests rely on SiteSetting email_domains_whitelist/blacklist being blank so the 'if (setting = ...).present?' branches never execute

adjudication.rationale: The new `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never sets `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`. In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the whitelist/blacklist checks are guarded by `(setting = ...).present?`, so with default/blank SiteSettings those branches won’t execute, meaning the relocated domain restriction logic from `User#email_validator` is not covered by the new spec.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The record.errors[attribute].blank? short-circuit guard in email_validator.rb:17-19 (block-check skipped when a restriction error already exists) has no test coverage; if the guard were inverted or removed, both spec examples would still pass

adjudication.rationale: email_validator.rb only runs the BlockedEmail check when `record.errors[attribute].blank?`. The spec does not cover the branch where a prior whitelist/blacklist restriction error exists, but the finding’s claim that “if the guard were inverted … both spec examples would still pass” is false: inverting the guard would prevent adding the blocked-email error when there are no prior errors, causing the “adds an error when email matches a blocked email” example to fail.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Every validator test stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the validator-to-model integration (the validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed? wiring in user.rb including the email_changed? conditional gate) is never exercised end-to-end; no test asserts a full user.valid? call adds user.email.blocked

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and invoke validator.validate_each directly, so the real BlockedEmail.should_block? path and the actual User model wiring (user.rb: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`) are not exercised via an end-to-end `user.valid?` call. The diff adds new behavior (BlockedEmail integration + conditional validation) but no spec asserts that a User validation run produces the `user.email.blocked` error when appropriate.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' test in blocked_email_spec.rb:28-31 only asserts absence, so it would also pass if should_block? returned nil instead of false on the missing-record path, failing to distinguish 'computed false' from 'no record' failure

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the missing-record path returns `record && ...`, which evaluates to `nil` when no record exists. The spec at lines 28-31 uses `subject.should be_false`, which in RSpec asserts the value is exactly `false` (not `nil`). So the test would *not* pass if `should_block?` returned `nil`; it would fail, meaning it does distinguish `false` from `nil`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_emails table ships with no writer path — nothing in the diff inserts rows (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed), leaving the feature inert in production

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails` (migration + `BlockedEmail` model) and enforces it via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within the shown changes there is no code path (controller/admin UI/API/rake task/seed) that creates or manages `BlockedEmail` rows—only specs fabricate them. This makes the new blocking mechanism effectively unused unless rows are inserted out-of-band (e.g., console/manual SQL), which is an incompleteness/operational concern rather than a direct correctness bug in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an unguarded write (increments match_count and updates last_match_at) from within validation, corrupting match statistics on every failed or aborted user save and double-counting when a record validates twice in one transaction

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no other email errors exist. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs a write side effect: it increments `match_count`, updates `last_match_at`, and `save`s whenever a matching record exists, regardless of whether the enclosing `User` save ultimately succeeds. Because model validations can run multiple times per save attempt or be re-run on failed/aborted saves, this can over-count and mutate stats simply due to validation being invoked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: last_match_at semantics are broken: since validations run before save, failed saves still burn a 'match', so last_match_at no longer means the email attempted signup but rather was ever validated against

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is invoked during validation (before persistence). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` unconditionally increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at` whenever a record exists, regardless of whether the enclosing `User` record ultimately saves successfully. Therefore, failed user creations (or any validation runs) will still update `last_match_at`, so it no longer strictly reflects a successful/committed signup attempt but any time the validator ran against that email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: action_type column has no DB default and the enum's zero value is invalid, so rows inserted via raw SQL/backfill either fail on MySQL strict mode or silently map to no enum member, causing blocklist entries to take do_nothing semantics instead of blocking

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` as `null: false` with **no DB default**, but the model sets a default in `before_validation` (`self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`). The finding’s key claim that the enum’s zero value is invalid is not supported: `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` implies `:block` is the first/zero value, so a raw-SQL insert that ends up with `0` would mean **block**, not `do_nothing`. Also, inserting without `action_type` would error due to `null: false` rather than “silently map to no enum member,” at least as shown by the schema in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Read-modify-write race in should_block? loses match-count increments under concurrent registrations (last write wins)

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; ...; record.save`) after fetching the row with `where(...).first`. Under concurrent calls, two processes can read the same `match_count`, both increment, and the later `save` overwrites the earlier one, losing an increment (and potentially clobbering `last_match_at`). This race is directly present in the added method in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: record.save in should_block? ignores the return value, silently swallowing save failures with no log or error

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a record is found it mutates `match_count`/`last_match_at` and calls `record.save` without checking the return value or handling failures (`app/models/blocked_email.rb`, lines adding `record.save`). Even though this likely won’t affect the boolean return (it still returns based on `action_type`), a failed save would silently skip updating the statistics with no visibility, which is a concrete robustness/observability issue grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client adds any email error (not just blocked) to rejectedEmails, permanently showing the wrong 'invalid' message instead of the actual server reason like not_allowed

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on any failed create where `result.errors.email` is present, the code pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), without checking the specific error type/message. Later, `emailValidation` short-circuits if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, overriding more specific server reasons like `user.email.not_allowed` or `user.email.blocked` coming from `users_controller.rb` (`errors: user.errors.to_hash`). Thus any email-related server error for that address causes the client to subsequently display the wrong generic “invalid” message for that email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Server locale user.email.blocked is dead on the client path; the client only renders the generic invalid message

adjudication.rationale: The new locale key `user.email.blocked` is not dead/unused: it is referenced by the new `EmailValidator` (`record.errors.add(attribute, I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked'))`) and will flow into the server-rendered error message (`user.errors.full_messages`) returned by `UsersController#create` as `message`. While the Ember controller does use the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` for its client-side revalidation when an email is in `rejectedEmails`, the diff does not show that `user.email.blocked` is intended to be rendered on the client, nor that it is unused overall.

adjudication_records.issue_text: rejectedEmails compares exact case, so case-variant emails bypass the cache and duplicate entries accumulate; should normalize with toLowerCase()

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new client-side cache uses `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` and stores values via `pushObject(result.values.email)`. Both operations are simple string comparisons with no normalization, so `Test@x.com` vs `test@x.com` will not match and the “already rejected” fast-fail won’t trigger. This can also allow multiple case-variant entries to accumulate in `rejectedEmails`. Server-side validation still applies, so it’s not a correctness/security defect, but it is a concrete UX/perf edge-case introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail stats DB write executes on every email validation including admin edits, adding an unnecessary unconditional write and making validation non-idempotent

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, when no prior email-domain restriction error exists it calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. That method performs a DB write whenever a `BlockedEmail` record exists: it increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s, even if the action is `:do_nothing` (it still updates stats). This makes validation have side effects / be non-idempotent and can add extra write load whenever an email matches a blocked-email entry (including during user updates where `email_changed?` is true). It’s not strictly incorrect behavior given the “stats” intent, but it is a meaningful architecture/perf concern created by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: DB error in the blocked-email write during validation escalates to StatementInvalid/rescued generic render, degrading the structured error response the client expects

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds DB interaction (including a write via `record.save`) inside `EmailValidator#validate_each` through `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb and app/models/blocked_email.rb). If that DB operation raises (e.g., `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid`), it will bypass the normal “validation failed” JSON render path in `UsersController#create` (which now includes `errors` and `values`) and instead hit the controller’s `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` path (response not shown in diff). That makes the structured `errors/values` payload non-guaranteed under DB failure. This is a real diff-grounded robustness concern, though it depends on exception behavior in the unseen rescue handler.
